newsitem.title: USA: Bad Rockies weather prevents flight for missing plane.
newsitem.headline: Bad Rockies weather prevents flight for missing plane.

text.p: Bad weather in the Rocky Mountains Tuesday again prevented an Air Force helicopter from reaching the snow-covered peak where the wreckage of a missing warplane is believed buried.
Air Force spokesman Lt. Keith Shepherd said snow at the higher elevations meant that a MH-53 heavy lift helicopter brought in to check the wreckage remained grounded Tuesday.

He said the helicopter, with a rescue-crew aboard, needed a three-hour window of opportunity to get up to the suspected crash site and remove some of the metal fragments spotted there to see if they came from the missing A-10 Thunderbolt.
Earlier in the day, a Colorado Air National Guard helicopter was able to fly up to the site and determined that the wreckage had not been completely covered by recent snow.

The wreckage of a plane that officials said was "likely" the missing aircraft was spotted on Sunday by an Army National Guard helicopter crew near a steep cliff on New York Mountain in the remote Sawatch Range southeast of the Vail ski resort.

The A-10 Thunderbolt disappeared during a routine training mission on April 2. Air Force officials have been at a loss to explain why the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, 32, left the three-plane delta formation and apparently veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles (1,350 km) from where the training exercise had been taking place.

Button, whose plane was carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) Mark 82 conventional bombs, broke away from the formation after leaving the Davis-Monthan Air Force Base near Tucson, Arizona, en route for the Barry M. Goldwater Bombing Range in Arizona.
